## Longitudinal cost data models

The following code runs models on the following outcomes as generated by the files in the `R/postmatch_processing.R` file, to calculate costs per month:

- Total costs 
- Physician/supplier costs
- Institutional total claims costs
- Institutional Home Health costs
- Institutional Inpatient costs
- Institutional Outpatient costs
- Institutional Skilled Nursing Facility costs
- Institutional Dialysis costs
- Institutional Auxiliary costs
- Institutional Hospice costs

Analyzing cost data is notoriously challenging [@mihaylova2011review]. The VA Health Economics Resource Center has a [practical guide](https://www.herc.research.va.gov/include/page.asp?id=analyzing-cost-data), and whole textbooks cover the topic [@deb2017econometrics].

To account for the repeated-observations nature of the data, both generalized estimating equations [@liang1986gee] and mixed-effects models with patient as a random effect [@laird1982random] were explored.

Medical cost data are highly skewed, with many zeros. We explored linear models, log(cost) models [@manning2001transform] and Tweedie models [@kurz2017tweedie].

Accounting for costs that are incomplete because follow-up ends, through loss of coverage or death, is itself a challenging topic, reviewed for health services researchers by Wijeysundera and colleagues [@wijeysundera2012censored]. Seminal methods papers include Lin and colleagues [@lin1997costs] and [Bang *et al*](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2673467).


We trialed multiple types of models:

- Naive estimation (patients do not contribute observations if uncovered or dead)
- Treating post-death costs as zero, ignoring months with costs uncovered (note: not done yet)
- Treating post-death costs as zero, weighting to adjust for uncovered months (note: not done yet)
